title: What is Peer-to-Peer architecture, and when is it the right fit (decentralization as a hard requirement: blockchain, file sharing, mesh)?
shortTitle: What is Peer-to-Peer architecture, and when is it the right fit?
keyPoints: In P2P every node is both client and server, communicating directly with peers and requiring no central authority.
The network self-organizes as peers join and leave, with no single point of control or failure.
Peer discovery, DHT-based routing, replication, and consensus protocols make the network function without a coordinator.
P2P is the right fit only when decentralization is a hard requirement, not a convenience.
Canonical use cases include blockchain, BitTorrent file sharing, and mesh or disaster-relief networks.
Consistency is much harder without a central authority, and security threats like Sybil attacks require dedicated countermeasures.
For the overwhelming majority of business systems, client-server with a load balancer is simpler and better.

s1_definition.oneliner: Every node is both client and server talking directly to peers with no central authority, which you choose only when decentralization itself is the requirement, as in blockchain, file sharing, and mesh networks.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Peer** – a node that acts as both a client and a server, capable of requesting work from others and serving work to others simultaneously.
- **Peer Discovery** – the mechanism by which a new node finds existing peers, often through a bootstrap list or a distributed directory.
- **DHT (Distributed Hash Table)** – a structured routing scheme like Kademlia that maps any key to a responsible peer, enabling lookups in about log(N) hops.
- **Replication** – storing each piece of data on multiple peers so that peers leaving does not lose data.
- **Consensus** – how peers agree on shared state without a central authority, using proof-of-work, proof-of-stake, or gossip protocols.
s1_definition.analogy: Normally National Bank of India has a central head office that every branch reports to and that is the single source of truth. In a peer-to-peer world there is no head office: each branch keeps its own copy of the shared ledger and talks directly to every other branch, and they agree on the truth by a majority voting protocol rather than by asking a boss. If one branch burns down, nothing is lost because every other branch has the full ledger.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Client-Server Model              Peer-to-Peer Model
  ────────────────────             ────────────────────

  ┌────────┐  ┌────────┐          ┌────────┐
  │Client A│  │Client B│          │ Peer A │◄────►┌────────┐
  └───┬────┘  └───┬────┘          └───┬────┘      │ Peer B │
      │           │                   │           └───┬────┘
      ▼           ▼                   │               │
  ┌──────────────────┐                ▼               ▼
  │     Server       │          ┌────────┐      ┌────────┐
  │ (single authority│          │ Peer C │◄────►│ Peer D │
  │  + bottleneck)   │          └────────┘      └────────┘
  └──────────────────┘
                                 Every peer talks to every peer.
  Server is SPOF.                No single point of failure.
  Server is bottleneck.          Each peer adds capacity.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Peer-to-Peer architecture makes every node both a client and a server, communicating directly with peers and requiring no central coordinator. The mechanisms that make it work are peer discovery, DHT-based routing for finding data, replication for surviving node departures, and consensus protocols for agreeing on shared state without a boss.

The deciding factor for choosing P2P is that decentralization must be a hard requirement. Blockchain exists precisely because no single party should control the ledger. BitTorrent uses it so there is no single server to overload or shut down. Mesh networks use it because there may be no central infrastructure at all. For a banking web application owned and operated by one bank, client-server with a load balancer is overwhelmingly simpler and better.

The trade-offs are real: consistency without a central authority requires slow consensus protocols, security is harder because of threats like Sybil attacks, and there is no central place to observe or debug the system. These costs are only worth paying when the absence of a central authority is the core requirement, not a preference.

Remember one sentence: choose P2P only when decentralization is a hard requirement, because for everything else, client-server is simpler and better.
